content: To achieve the goals of strengthening health workforce (HWF) data, evidence, and knowledge, the Global Strategy on Human Resources for Health (GSHRH) outlines several objectives. These include the enhancement of national health workforce registries, which are critical for monitoring workforce capacity and dynamics. Sharing data, indicators, and accounts on the health workforce between countries is also emphasized as essential. Member States are urged to establish or improve national health personnel information systems to collect and analyze reliable, up-to-date health workforce data. Such data can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of health workforce policies and translate findings into actionable plans. The High-Level Commission on Health Employment and Economic Growth, in alignment with the GSHRH, published a report titled Working for Health and Growth in 2016. This report includes a five-year action plan aimed at promoting health employment and inclusive economic growth. The plan is supported by the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), and the World Health Organization (WHO). The Seventieth World Health Assembly reviewed this report and recommended implementing the Commission’s recommendations. The Commission’s vision is to accelerate progress toward universal health coverage (UHC) and the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) by ensuring equitable access to health workers within robust health systems. The Commission proposed ten recommendations to transform national health workforces to meet the SDGs and develop labor market policies accordingly. Achieving a fit-for-purpose health workforce requires coordinated actions across all sectors involved in the health labor market. This includes access to data, indicators, and health workforce accounts, as well as the capacity to analyze these data for labor market insights. Recommendation 10 of the action plan emphasizes the need for robust research and analysis of health labor markets using harmonized metrics and methodologies to strengthen evidence, accountability, and action. This aligns with the GSHRH milestones, highlighting the urgency of immediate action on data, indicators, and health workforce accounts, and the necessity of harmonized metrics and methodologies across nations. The National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) framework supports countries in achieving these goals. It facilitates the rapid aggregation and display of health workforce data for decision-making and serves as a tool to guide evidence-based health workforce policy decisions. The NHWA also supports labor market analysis, policy design, and the evaluation of policy impacts. Additionally, it tracks and supports countries’ efforts toward UHC, the SDGs, and the GSHRH milestones by creating a harmonized approach for timely data collection, improving information architecture and interoperability, and defining core indicators for strategic workforce planning and global monitoring. At the national level, the NHWA provides several benefits. It offers a comprehensive understanding of the health workforce, including its size, characteristics, and distribution, enabling countries to identify needs and opportunities for strengthening their workforce. High-quality information from the NHWA informs evidence-based policy decisions tailored to country-specific needs. It also supports the transformation and scaling-up of health workforce education and training to achieve UHC. Furthermore, the NHWA fosters intersectoral policy dialogue among relevant ministries, such as those of education, health, and finance, to strengthen policies, strategies, and plans. Cross-cutting investments in all NHWA modules promote data-driven planning, capacity-building, and systematic research on health system developments and resilience planning. The NHWA inspires countries to address critical policy questions related to health workforce challenges and optimize planning systems. For example, it helps assess whether the current workforce is adequate in terms of availability, accessibility, acceptability, and competence to deliver quality health services. It also explores strategies to address workforce gaps through better resource allocation, increased productivity, effective retention policies, and public-private partnerships. Additionally, it examines how investments in education and production or increased in-migration can address workforce shortages. The NHWA also evaluates the financial feasibility of policies aimed at improving workforce performance and increasing inputs, including negotiations with governments and the private sector. At the regional level, the NHWA enhances the comparability of health workforce data across countries, facilitating capacity-building, information exchange, and research on future workforce trends. The NHWA framework aligns closely with the health labor market framework for UHC, which integrates education, labor market dynamics, and societal drivers to achieve UHC and optimal healthcare services. It provides actionable directions for health workforce policies that contribute to the GSHRH milestones, UHC, and the SDGs. The NHWA framework includes ten modules, each addressing specific aspects of the health workforce. For instance, Module 1 focuses on the active health workforce stock, providing a detailed overview of workforce composition and distribution. This module helps identify gaps in professions or competencies and mismatches in geographical or sectoral distribution, enabling targeted policy interventions. Modules 2, 3, and 4 address education and training, supporting the sustainable expansion and reform of health workforce education to increase its quantity, quality, and relevance. These modules guide efforts to reorient the workforce toward addressing social determinants of health, health promotion, disease prevention, primary care, and integrated, community-based services. The NHWA’s modular approach allows countries to prioritize and implement modules based on their specific needs and goals. While the full implementation of all ten modules provides comprehensive coverage, countries can adopt a flexible approach, selecting indicators and modules that align with their immediate priorities. Over time, as more indicators become available, countries can achieve a more detailed understanding of their health workforce landscape, enabling sophisticated analyses, efficient policies, and progress toward UHC.
